title: Entlöftet: Meine Verteidigung gegen Ciceros Diffamierungen
excerpt: Cicero hat die Verschwörung entlöftet und versucht, mich vor dem Senat zu diskreditieren. Aber ich werde nicht feige sein oder mich entschuldigen. Ich habe nach Gerechtigkeit gehandelt und werde meine Position verteidigen, koste es, was es wolle.
author: catilina

content.diary:
It is done. Cicero has risen in the Senate and made his accusations public. In his theatrical way, he has condemned me as a traitor, painted me as a man who would burn Rome to ashes for personal ambition. The dramatic orator, always aware of his audience, has performed masterfully.

And yet his accusations, for all their eloquence, contain distortions and lies. Yes, I have organized people. Yes, there are those willing to support radical change. But his portrayal of my intentions—as though I wished to sack Rome, murder senators wholesale, install myself as dictator—this is caricature designed to horrify rather than illuminate.

I could stand in the Senate and defend myself, could offer counter-arguments to his accusations. But would it matter? The Senate is already half-convinced by Cicero's eloquence. They fear change; they cling to the system that has served their interests. They will accept Cicero's narrative because it justifies their resistance to reform.

So I choose a different path. I will not dignify Cicero's accusations with detailed rebuttal. Instead, I am leaving Rome. I am going to join Manlius and the forces in Etruria. There, we will gather strength, and from a position of military power, we will resume the struggle for justice.

Let Cicero boast of his exposure of the conspiracy. Let the Senate feel temporarily secure in their narrow victory. These moments of triumph are brief. The underlying problems—the debt-crushed masses, the excluded young men, the soldiers without land—these problems remain. The structure that created the conditions for conspiracy is unchanged.

I am not afraid. I have known for some time that Cicero posed a threat to my plans. This exposure was perhaps inevitable. But I am not destroyed; my supporters are not all arrested; the forces we have gathered still exist.

I will lead them. Whether history remembers me as a failed revolutionary or as a visionary reformer depends on what happens next. But I refuse to be remembered as a coward who abandoned his principles when challenged.

The road ahead is uncertain and dangerous. But it is my road, and I will walk it to its end, whatever that end may be.
content.scientific:
After Cicero's exposure of the conspiracy, Catilina faced a critical decision point. Rather than remaining in Rome to face senatorial action or arrest, he chose to flee and join Manlius and the military forces in Etruria. This decision transformed the conspiracy from an urban political plot into an armed rebellion.

Historians view Catilina's departure from Rome and subsequent military mobilization as indicating that the conspiracy had reached a critical point. Whether the timing was chosen (Catilina deciding to accelerate the uprising) or forced (circumstances compelling him to act before he intended) remains historically unclear. The practical result was that Catilina became identifiable as a rebel in arms against the state—a position far more serious than the conspiracy charge he faced in Rome.

quote.text: Ciceronis eloquentia timeo, sed veritate vinco.
quote.translation: I fear Cicero's eloquence, but I conquer through truth.
quote.author: Lucius Sergius Catilina
